paras: Every profession that sells judgement is now being told that judgement is about to be automated, and lawyers are hearing it more loudly than most. The honest place to begin is by acknowledging what the optimists have got right, because on the tasks where the output can be checked against a known answer the machines are already faster and, arguably, more consistent than the people they are compared with. Anybody who has watched a first-year associate spend a weekend on a document review knows that this is not a small claim. It would be easy, and dishonest, to open with the objection.

The counterargument is not that the technology is weak. It is that the tasks being measured are the ones that were always easiest to measure, which is a familiar problem in any industry, and the conclusion drawn from them is far broader than the evidence supports. Notwithstanding the results, almost none of the published tests examine the part of professional work that consumes the most hours: deciding which question is actually being asked. A client does not arrive with a question. He arrives with a situation and a mood, and the first hour is spent finding out what he is really worried about. Whereas a document review has a right answer, that hour does not, and nothing yet measures it.

On balance, then, the sensible position is neither of the two on offer. The tools are compelling and they are being sold with claims that do not hold water, and both of those things are true at once. Admittedly, saying so satisfies nobody: it is read as complacency by one side and as hype by the other. The blind spot is shared, though, and it is this. Everybody is arguing about whether the work can be done faster, while nobody is arguing about who is responsible when it is done wrong, and that second question is the one that will decide how any of this is used. Until it is answered, every prediction should be qualified, however confidently it is delivered.

listenings.text: I write the objection first. Not the introduction, not the argument, the objection: the single strongest thing somebody could say against me, in one paragraph, put as well as they would put it. Then I write the piece around it. There are two reasons and only one of them is honourable. The honourable one is that if the objection destroys my argument, I have found out on a Tuesday afternoon instead of in public, and I have saved myself three weeks. The other reason is tactical, and I am not proud of it. A reader who sees his own objection stated better than he could state it stops looking for the trap. He relaxes, and he reads the rest of the piece as an argument rather than as a fight. The strange part, after twenty years of doing this, is how often the objection turns out to be right and the piece I meant to write turns into a different piece entirely.

I changed my mind in public once, on a panel, in front of about four hundred people, and I would recommend it to nobody and I would not undo it. What happened was that somebody on the other side made an argument I had genuinely never heard, and I could feel myself reaching for the answer I had prepared, and the answer did not fit. There is a silence of about four seconds in the recording. What I said was that I would have to think about it, which sounds weak and was the only true thing available. Two people came up to me afterwards and told me it was the most persuasive thing anybody said all afternoon, which I found infuriating, because I had lost. The lesson I took is narrower than people expect. It is not that you should change your mind. It is that you should notice, out loud, when an argument has landed, because everybody in the room already noticed.
